newsitem.title: UK: British Airways reports record third-quarter profit.
newsitem.headline: British Airways reports record third-quarter profit.

text.p: British Airways Plc celebrated 10 years in the private sector a day early Monday with the announcement of record third-quarter pretax profits, marred only by a sharp rise in jet fuel prices.

It said higher passenger and cargo traffic helped boost pre-tax profits for the three months by 8.7 percent to 113 million pounds ($184.4 million). Revenues gained 6.3 percent to 2.02 billion pounds ($3.3 billion).
The pre-tax result for the nine months to Dec. 31 rose to an all-time high of 583 million pounds ($953 million), up from last year's record 534 million ($873 million) for the same period.
But third-quarter operating profits slipped to 131 million pounds ($214 million) from 152 million ($248 million) a year ago due to higher fuel prices.
BA said operating profits would have been up 23 percent but for a 33.7 percent rise in the quarterly fuel bill to 222 million pounds ($363 million).
The results came in ahead of most market forecasts of around 100 million pounds ($163 million) pre-tax for the third quarter.
"The cost items were much better than expected," said analyst James Halstead at brokers Credit Lyonnais Laing.

"These are very, very good results," said Chris Avery at Paribas Capital Markets. However, he cautioned that there were likely to be some costs to come in the full-year results from recently announced job cuts.
BA plans to make a progress report on its campaign to find a billion pounds ($1.6 billion) of annual cost savings when it reports full-year results in May, Chief Executive Robert Ayling said.

Chairman Sir Colin Marshall said in his results statement that the cost-cutting programme was on track and he expected the trends behind the economic growth and record profits seen in the airline industry in 1996 to continue in 1997.
BA launched an efficiency programme last September.

Since then it has announced various moves to sell off or reorganize parts of the business, such as ground services and cargo handling. But Ayling said it was too early to give a running tally of savings so far.
Ayling said much still had to be done if the airline was to remain competitive, saying that operating margins at rival U.S. carriers were higher.
BA's scheduled passenger traffic in the third quarter was up 9.1 percent, with the average number of seats sold rising to a record 71.2 percent of capacity from 70.7 percent a year ago.

The airline said the average fare yield for every kilometre flown dipped 1.8 percent due to the strength of sterling but overall the effects of moves in exchange rates on costs and sales were largely neutral.
Fuel prices were the main factor behind a 0.3 percent increase in unit costs, which otherwise would have fallen 3 percent due to increased efficiencies, the airline said.

Marshall did not comment on the proposed alliance with American Airlines except to say BA would also concentrate this year "on completing the regulatory clearance of the alliance with American Airlines and launch the resultant enhanced services across the North Atlantic."

The controversial deal, which would see BA and American controlling more than 60 percent of the British transatlantic market, has come under heavy fire from rival airlines as well as from the European Commission and some consumer groups.
